coastal-landscapes: The Holderness cliffs have been crumbling into the North Sea for centuries. Where does all that material go?
Between 1951 and 2004 the cliffs at Aldbrough, on England's Holderness coast, retreated about 2 m a year. Why do they disappear so fast?
In 1990 an Australian sea arch fell, stranding two visitors on a new island. How does the sea make islands?
Spurn Point is over three miles long and in places only 50 m wide. How did a finger of sand form across the mouth of the Humber?
The sea is wrecking the rock towers that millions of visitors come to see. Should anyone try to stop it?
Some of an English estuary's mud comes from crumbling cliffs up the coast. How does that mud become land?
On the coast of the Gulf of Bothnia, the land rises out of the sea by about 0.9 m a century. Elsewhere, coasts are drowning. How can both be true?
By 2014 the Environment Agency had built new banks inland at Medmerry, West Sussex, and let the sea flood the land between. Why give land to the sea?
In 1917 the sea destroyed a Devon fishing village. Why did a local newspaper blame a naval dockyard?
glaciated-landscapes: Between 1941 and 2004, Alaska's Muir Glacier retreated 12 km. All that time, its ice kept flowing towards the sea. How can both be true?
Some glaciers race forward metres a day. Others, frozen to their beds, barely move. Why the difference?
Yosemite's Lembert Dome has a gentle slope on one side and a steep face on the other. Why?
A 16,500-tonne boulder sits on the flat prairie of Alberta, Canada, far from the mountains it came from. How did it get there?
In May 2025 a glacier buried much of the Swiss village of Blatten. Why did only one person die?
Greenland's largest outlet glacier more than doubled its speed in about a decade. What controls an ice-sheet landscape?
How can a ridge of river gravel wind uphill and over hills, when rivers only flow downhill?
Near Tuktoyaktuk in Arctic Canada, a 49 m hill rises out of flat tundra. Its core is solid ice. How did it form?
About half of the 800-mile Trans-Alaska Pipeline runs above the ground. Why not bury all of it?
For a century, two dams stood on a river draining glaciated mountains. Why did the beach at its mouth shrink?
dryland-landscapes: Antarctica is covered in ice, yet it counts as a desert. How?
Sand covers only about 20% of the world's deserts. What shapes the rest?
Death Valley gets almost no rain. So what built its landscape?
In the Namib, a river that flows only every few years stops a sea of giant dunes. How can that be?
Why do deserts hold landforms that today's dry climate could never have made?
From the 1960s, irrigation turned Central Asian desert into cotton fields. Later, the Aral Sea largely dried up and fields turned salty. How can watering a desert damage it?
In Utah's desert, damaged ground can take decades to heal. How can off-road driving reshape a whole landscape?
earths-life-support-systems: At any moment, rivers hold only about 0.006% of Earth's fresh water. So how does a river keep flowing through weeks without rain?
Most of Earth's carbon is locked away in rock. How does any of it get back into the air?
Clear the Amazon's trees and the streams run fuller. So why could the region end up drier?
Arctic tundra soils have built up a vast store of carbon. Why is the tundra now giving some back?
Pump out ancient groundwater, burn ancient carbon: what happens when we take faster than a cycle refills?
Since 1979 the Arctic has warmed nearly four times as fast as the planet as a whole. Why there?
The air in a forest changes between day and night. How do scientists spot the slow change hidden underneath?
Forests, peat bogs and farm soils all lock up carbon. Can the whole world agree to protect them?
Since 1970 the world has lost about 22% of its wetlands. Can a plan for a whole river basin bring a wetland back?
changing-spaces-making-places: Is a place just a dot on a map, or something more?
Your street has a story no map tells. How do you uncover what made your own place what it is?
A crowded ward on the edge of a global city: how do you study a place thousands of miles away?
A poet begged bombs to fall on a town. Can a poem change how a real place is seen and treated?
In 2011, 1 in 10 people in Mumbai's D ward lived in slums. In M/East ward, more than 3 in 4 did. Why such a gap inside one city?
Detroit had 1,849,568 people in 1950 and 639,111 in 2020. What emptied the Motor City?
Redcar's carbon emissions plunged in just two years. Why did nobody celebrate?
Why would a city spend millions on a year of art?
Two neighbourhoods on two continents: both were demolished and redeveloped. Who decides what replaces a neighbourhood?
Hull was UK City of Culture in 2017. Years later, how could anyone prove whether it worked?
global-systems-trade-in-the-contemporary: If goods still dominate world trade, why have services and trade between developing countries grown faster?
Vietnam's exports have grown more than 160-fold since 1990. Does trade build development for everyone?
In 2023 the Panama Canal cut the number of ships it let through. In 2026 conflict choked oil shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Has technology really made the world "shrink"?

Apple employs about 166,000 people. Toyota and its affiliates run more than 50 manufacturing operations in 27 countries and regions outside Japan. Why do these two giants make their products in such different ways?
Why do most EU countries trade more with each other than with the rest of the world?
India sells most to the USA but buys most from China. What does two-way trade do to a fast-growing country?
The UK has bought more than it sold almost every year since 1998. So how can it still shape world trade?
Ethiopia imports almost six times the value of goods it exports. Why can't it simply sell more goods?
global-systems-global-migration: Only about one person in 27 is an international migrant. Why do some people move while most stay?
In 2024 one inflow of money into Tajikistan equalled almost half of its GDP. Which flows matter most, and for which places?
Within a year of August 2017, nearly 725,000 people had fled from Myanmar into Bangladesh. Why do so many people flee at once, and what happens where they arrive?
From 1 January 2021, EU citizens needed points to get a UK work visa. By the year to March 2023, UK net migration had peaked at 944,000. How far can governments control global interactions?
18.5 million people born in India live in other countries, more than from any other country. How do they change places at both ends?
UK net migration fell from 944,000 to 171,000 in under three years. Who decides how many people come?
Money worth a quarter of Nepal's GDP arrives from people who have left. Who sets the rules for that money?
global-governance-human-rights: Forty-eight countries voted for the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Did that bind any of them?
Why are forced labour, maternal deaths and executions concentrated in such different places?
Nearly half of the 2.4 million elected members of India's rural local councils are women. Can reserving places close a development gap?
When a government abuses its own people, who has the right to step in, and how?
Over a million Rohingya refugees live in camps in Bangladesh. Who is responsible for protecting their rights?
Most of Rwanda's MPs are women, yet it is rated "Not Free". Has human rights governance there succeeded?
global-governance-power-and-borders: Taiwan elects its own government. So why does it have no seat at the United Nations?
In 2014, one of Apple's Irish subsidiaries paid tax at an effective rate of 0.005% on its profits. How is that possible, and who loses?

Between 1970 and 2008 the share of world trade in world GDP more than doubled. Since then it has stalled, moving between about 52% and 62% to 2024, and nationalist politics has grown. Is globalisation creating its own backlash?
Why do some ethnic tensions end in a peace deal, and others in war or a divided country?
In 2014 and again in 2022, most UN members voted that Ukraine's borders still stood. Why couldn't the votes protect them?
States promise never to use force against each other. So why do they still intervene, and at what cost?
In 2013, tens of thousands of South Sudanese fled into UN bases. Who protects and supports them today?
In 2000, rebels seized hundreds of UN peacekeepers in Sierra Leone. Could outside governance bring peace?
climate-change: Air bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice are up to 800,000 years old. What can they tell us about past climate?
In 1991 one volcano in the Philippines cooled the whole planet. How?
Global sea level has risen about 10 cm since 1993, and the yearly rise has more than doubled. Where is the extra water coming from?
The UK's emissions fell by 54% between 1990 and 2025. Has the UK really halved its part in climate change?
Scientists linked carbon dioxide to warming in the 1890s. Why was it still argued over a century later?
No one knows how much coal, oil and gas the world will burn. So how can anyone forecast the climate of 2100?
In June 2021 a Canadian village reached 49.6 °C, a national record. Could that have happened without climate change?
Since the 1950s, many upper-ocean species have moved towards the poles by about 52 km every decade. Why move, and what happens to living things and farms on land?
About a quarter of the Netherlands lies below sea level. Tuvalu's land averages about 2 m above it. Which is more vulnerable, and why?

In May 2024 a company opened what it called the world's largest plant for pulling CO₂ out of the air, in Iceland, designed to capture up to 36,000 tonnes a year. Could machines like it clean up our emissions?
A Louisiana island has lost almost all its land, and its people are moving. When is moving the best plan?
The least developed countries emitted less than 0.4% of all historical fossil CO₂, yet face some of the worst impacts. Who should cut emissions, and who should pay?
disease-dilemmas: In 2000, non-communicable diseases caused 58% of the world's deaths. In 2023 they caused 74%. Good news or bad news?
In October 2010, cholera was reported in Haiti. By February 2019 there had been 820,000 cases. How did it arrive, and why did it spread so fast?
Malaria killed an estimated 610,000 people in 2024. Why does it kill mostly in one continent, and mostly young children?
Why are some diseases turning up in places, seasons and animals where they were never found before?
Some people who have never smoked get lung cancer. Can a country clean its air enough to prevent it?
In 1961 heart and circulatory disease caused over half of all UK deaths. Why has its death rate fallen so far?

In September 2019 a global board warned: "The world is not prepared" for a fast-moving respiratory pandemic. Months later came COVID-19. Why did a warned world still lose an estimated 14.9 million lives in 2020 and 2021?
How do you fight a deadly outbreak in rainforest villages hundreds of kilometres from the nearest city?
New HIV infections have fallen 65% since their peak in 1994. Was that prevention or treatment, and why are some groups still left behind?
The bark of an African mountain tree is shipped abroad as a medicine. Can the trade last without losing the tree?
A vaccine developed in Oxford was also made in India and Korea. How does one drug company reach the world?
exploring-oceans: If you drained the oceans, what landscape would you see on the sea floor?
The Gulf Stream carries more water than all the world's rivers combined. Is that why north-west Europe has mild winters?
Sunlight reaches only the top of the ocean. So how does anything live in the deep?
The world now farms more fish and shellfish than it catches. Does that solve overfishing?
The ocean holds oil, gas, moving water and metal-rich rocks. Which of them could we run out of?
Russia, Denmark and Canada have each asked a UN body to recognise their seabed rights in the Arctic Ocean. Who owns the ocean floor?
future-of-food: In 2023 the world's food supply came to about 3,000 calories per person per day. So why did around 645 million people go hungry in 2025?
On the journey from field to fork, where does so much of the world's food go missing?
Strawberries in December, and food prices that spike worldwide at once. Is global food a gift or a risk?
In 1798, Thomas Malthus argued that population would outrun food. Since 1961, the world's population has grown about 2.6 times. Has food per person risen or fallen?
Early warning systems forecast a likely emergency in Somalia in August 2010. Famine was declared in July 2011. Why did a warning not prevent disaster?

In March, April and May 2026, oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz averaged about 2.7 million barrels a day, down from about 20 million. Why did farmers and food importers far from the Gulf feel the shock?
Between 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, the Sahara had permanent lakes, plants and people. Today it is desert. Did people cause the change?
How can warm water in the Pacific leave families in southern Africa short of food?
Shishmaref, an Iñupiaq village on an Alaskan island, has voted three times to move. Why, and why is it still there?
hazardous-earth: Coal in Antarctica, fossils across an ocean: what finally proved that continents move?
The Atlantic is about 2.5 cm wider every year. What moves the plates?
In 1985 a volcano 45 km away killed about 23,000 people in Armero, two hours after it erupted. How?
After a 2004 earthquake off Sumatra, people died in 10 countries around the Indian Ocean. How?
About 1,600 magnitude-5 earthquakes strike each year, and about one magnitude-8. Which should planners prepare for?
On Fuego, in 2018, a golf resort evacuated safely. A village two kilometres further on was buried. Why?
Nepal 2015 and Kaikōura 2016 were both magnitude 7.8. One killed more than 8,790 people; the other killed 2. Why?
By 2013, Hong Kong said it had cut the landslide risk from its man-made slopes by about 75%. Is preventing disasters worth more than responding to them?
Large earthquakes are not becoming more common. So why do experts expect more people to be affected by geophysical disasters?
exploring-oceans-part-2: Tankers spilled about 95% less oil in the 2010s than in the 1970s. Why has plastic proved so much harder to stop?
When an oil well blew out under the sea, why did hotels far from any oil lose bookings?
The ocean took up 29% of the CO₂ humans emitted over the last decade. Why is that bad news for coral reefs?
The sea around a Pacific island nation is rising faster than the world average. What can its people do?
Several countries have asked the UN for more Arctic seabed. Why does shrinking sea ice make it worth claiming?
In 2024, ships from Shenzhen to Rotterdam began sailing about 3,000 extra nautical miles around Africa. Why take the long way?
Why are a few stretches of sea so dangerous, both for ships and for people seeking safety?
future-of-food-part-2: In January 2018 Cape Town, a city of just over 4 million people, warned that its taps could be turned off in April: "Day Zero". What pushed it to the edge, and how did it pull back?
Soy fields have replaced rainforest in Mato Grosso. Why might the farms themselves end up paying for it?
In 2022, 149 million young children were stunted while 2.5 billion adults were overweight. How can the world have too little food and too much at once?
What does going without enough food mean for a family in the UK, and for one in Somalia?
Who really decides what ends up on your plate: farmers, governments or supermarkets?
Brazil left the UN's Hunger Map in 2014, fell back onto it, then left again in 2025. What does it take to end hunger, and to keep it ended?
